name: Gyeong
description: Gyeong is a hopping vampire from East Asian folklore, sharing many characteristics with the Chinese jiangshi, on which it is based. The jiangshi legend originated in China during the Qing Dynasty and spread throughout East Asia, including Korea, where this specific variant acquired local characteristics. The term "gyeong" is associated with reanimated corpses that lack the ability to bend their joints due to rigor mortis, forcing them to move by hopping with their arms extended forward. According to Taoist-influenced folklore, a jiangshi is created when a persons soul (hun) fails to leave the body after death, often due to improper burial, suicide, or death under unnatural circumstances. The corpse becomes animated by residual qi energy and seeks to absorb the life force (yang energy) from the living to sustain its unnatural existence. These creatures were particularly feared in rural communities where proper burial rites were essential to ensuring the peaceful transition of the deceased
source: Korean folklore; a vampire-like creature similar to the jiangshi.

name: Gygrid
description: Gygrid (plural: gygrier) is a female giant or troll-woman in Norwegian folklore, from Old Norse gygr meaning ogress. The gygrid is a mountain-dwelling giantess, often associated with specific mountains in Vestlandet. Unlike male giants (jøtuler) who throw boulders, the gygrid is more subtle — she uses magic, seduction, and trickery. Some gygrier were said to be beautiful and would marry human men, but the marriage always came with a terrible price. Others were hideous hags who kidnapped children and travelers. Many Vestlandet mountains are said to be gygrier turned to stone when caught by the sunrise. The name appears in Norwegian place names throughout Vestlandet — Gygrehola, Gygrestolen, and Gygreskaret. The gygrid is distinct from the hulder (a forest spirit) — the gygrid is larger, more ancient, and more closely connected to the raw mountain landscape. She represents the untamed female power of the Norwegian mountains
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Haetae
description: Haetae (also known as Haechi) is a mythical guardian beast from Korean mythology, depicted as a chimeric lion-like creature covered in scales with a single horn on its forehead. It is one of the most important and beloved mythical creatures in Korean culture, serving as the official symbol of Seoul. Haetae are believed to possess the ability to distinguish good from evil, making them symbols of justice and law. They are also fire-eating guardians, capable of neutralizing destructive fire energy (hwa-gi) and preventing fires. During the Joseon Dynasty, haetae statues were placed in front of Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul to counter the fire energy emanating from Mount Gwanaksan. The haetae also served as the official emblem of the Saheonbu (Office of the Inspector General), with officials wearing its image to project incorruptibility. In legend, when two people fought, the haetae would gore the dishonest one with its horn, making it an ultimate arbiter of truth In North Korea folklore, this figure is known among the North Korea people.
source: https://www.mcst.go.kr/english/policy/kocis/newsView.jsp?pSeq=85 / https://koccult.com/creatures/haetae / https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haetae

source: Korean mythology; the Haetae is a guardian beast that distinguishes truth from lies.

name: Haggs
description: Haggs are malevolent spirits from the folklore of the Isle of Man, a self-governing Crown dependency located in the Irish Sea between England and Ireland. These supernatural entities are closely related to the hags and witches found throughout Celtic mythology but possess distinct characteristics unique to Manx tradition. On the Isle of Man, the Haggs is often associated with the "Mooinjer Veggey," the Little People or fairies, though it is considered a more harmful member of the fairy community. Manx folklore is rich with tales of supernatural beings that inhabit the islands hills, glens, and shorelines, and the Haggs occupies a particularly feared position as a bringer of misfortune. Like many Manx creatures, the Haggs is most active during the twilight hours and on festival nights such as Hop-tu-Naa (the Manx Halloween). The belief in such creatures was once widespread among the rural farming communities who relied on oral tradition to pass down warnings and protective measures
source: Saint Vincent folklore — spirit documented in Saint Vincent oral tradition.

name: Haint
description: A Haint is a restless or malevolent spirit in African American and Gullah Geechee folklore. The term derives from the Gullah pronunciation of 'haunt' and encompasses a broad category of supernatural entities — including the spirits of the dead, Boo Hags, Plat-Eyes, and other wandering entities. Haints are believed to be souls that cannot rest due to unfinished business, improper burial, or violent death. The most distinctive cultural response to haints is 'haint blue' — a pale blue-green paint used on porch ceilings, window trim, and door frames to confuse and repel spirits. In Gullah belief, haints cannot cross water, and the blue color mimics water or sky, creating a barrier they cannot breach. Haints represent the deep connection between African American spiritual traditions and West African ancestor veneration
source: Charles C. Jones, Negro Myths from the Georgia Coast (1888)

name: Háldi
description: Háldi (plural Háldit) are nature spirits in Sami animistic belief, the guardians and protectors of specific places, animals, and plants. Each natural location — a lake, a fell, a forest, a stretch of river — has its own háldi who must be respected and propitiated. They are generally benevolent but can cause trouble if offended. Some háldit are associated with sacrificial stones called sieidi. The háldi tradition reflects the Sami belief that all significant natural objects possess a soul. Humans could marry háldi beings — stories tell of men marrying háldi women from invisible parallel worlds, marriages that often came with strict taboos. There are sea háldit (čáhceháldit), forest háldit, and mountain háldit, each governing different domains. The háldi differs from the Ulda in that háldit are tied to specific natural features rather than constituting a separate underground people
source: University of Minnesota Press; saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; Wikipedia (Sami mythology)

name: Halmasti
description: Halmasti, also known as the Celestial Hound, is a terrifying wolf-like creature from Chitrali folklore in northern Pakistan. Its name derives from the Khowar language and means 'thunder,' reflecting its association with destructive lightning and violent celestial forces. Halmasti is deeply connected to liminal moments in life, appearing during births and deaths when spiritual vulnerability is highest. The legend represents a unique synthesis of Sumerian, Semitic, Iranic, Turkic, and Chinese mythological traditions, with origins tracing back to the ancient Sumerian female demon Littu, which evolved into Lilith in Semitic mythology, became Al or Hal in Iranic tradition, and Al-Basti in Turkic culture. The Chitrali version absorbed elements from the Chinese Tiangou (Heavenly Dog), a celestial hound that descends with thunder to cause eclipses
source: Pakistani folklore — beast documented in Pakistani oral tradition.

name: Hanako-san
description: Hanako-san (also known as Toire no Hanako-san or Hanako of the Toilet) is one of the most famous Japanese urban legends, dating back to the 1950s. The legend tells of the ghost of a young girl who haunts school bathrooms, particularly on the third floor of elementary and middle schools across Japan. The story has become a staple of Japanese schoolyard folklore, passed down through generations of children as a test of courage. Variations of the legend exist in different regions, with some versions claiming Hanako was killed during World War II air raids, others saying she was murdered by a stranger in the bathroom, and some stating she was a victim of bullying. The legend reflects broader Japanese folk beliefs about spirits (yurei) of children who died tragically and remain bound to places associated with their death
source: Japanese urban legend; the ghost of a girl haunting school bathrooms.

name: Hang Tuah (The Invincible Warrior)
description: Hang Tuah is the most legendary warrior in Malay history and folklore, the paragon of Malay chivalry and loyalty. According to the Malay Annals (Sejarah Melayu), he served as the Laksamana (admiral) of the Melaka Sultanate during its golden age in the 15th century under Sultan Mansur Shah. Hang Tuah was unmatched in silat, diplomacy, and statesmanship. Together with four other legendary warriors (Hang Jebat, Hang Kasturi, Hang Lekir, and Hang Lekiu), he defended Melaka's sovereignty. His most famous tale involves being falsely accused of adultery with a palace maid and sentenced to death. His executioner spared him, and when Hang Jebat rebelled against the Sultan, Hang Tuah was recalled to kill his closest friend. Hang Tuah's legendary kris (dagger), Taming Sari, was said to give him invincibility in battle
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hang_Tuah

name: Hans Uredd
description: Hans Uredd (Fearless Hans) is a folk hero from Norwegian folktales, particularly associated with Trøndelag versions of the AT326 (The Boy Who Didn't Know What Fear Was) tale type. The story features a young man from a Trøndelag farm who is so fearless that he cannot understand what fear means. His quest to 'learn to shudder' takes him through encounters with supernatural beings — trolls, ghosts, the Draug, and the Dead Man's Mass — that are specifically placed in Trøndelag landscapes. Versions of the tale were collected in Trøndelag by folklorists and feature localized elements: the hero visits Trondheim, encounters trolls in Trollheimen, and crosses the Trondheimsfjord. The name 'Hans Uredd' (Hans the Fearless) has become synonymous in Norwegian with someone who shows extraordinary courage in the face of supernatural danger
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Hanuman
description: Hindu monkey god, commander of monkey army in Ramayana. SON of Anjana (celestial apsara) + Kesari (Vanara chieftain), blessed by Vayu Deva (wind god). Baby: tried to grab Sun (thought it was fruit), Indra struck his JAW (hanu) with thunderbolt - Name from 'hanu' (jaw) + 'man' (disfigured). Sage Curse: forgot powers (flight, infinite size) until reminded. Supernatural Powers: shapeshift, fly, increase size, immense strength, speed, mastery of Vedas. Ramayana: led monkeys to help Rama (Vishnu avatar) rescue Sita from Ravana. Leaps across ocean to Lanka, carries message, Sets Fire to Lanka with burning tail, Flies to Himalayas for medicinal mountain to save Lakshmana. Temple: monkey with red face, stands erect. Model for bhakti (devotion). Hanuman Chalisa (40 verses by Tulsidas) recited daily. Worship: entry guard, protect from evil, warriors, athletes. Also inspired Chinese Journey to the West (Journey to the West)
source: Hindu mythology, Vedas, Puranas & Mahabharata

name: Hawk Guardian of Ojibwe
description: In the Canadian territories of the Ojibwe people, the Hawk Guardian takes on distinct characteristics shaped by the boreal forests and countless lakes of Ontario, Manitoba, and beyond. This manifestation of the Hawk Guardian is particularly associated with the northern woodlands, where the harsh winters demand exceptional survival skills and community cooperation. The Canadian Ojibwe have deep connections to this spirit through ceremonies that mark the changing seasons and the cycles of plant and animal life. The Hawk Guardian in this region is especially revered during the harvesting of wild rice and maple sap, when its presence signals that the time is right for these traditional activities. Ojibwe communities across Canada maintain the sacred stories of the Hawk Guardian as part of their living cultural heritage In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) spiritual tradition; documented in Great Lakes ethnographic records.

name: Hawk Spirit of Blackfoot
description: The Hawk Spirit of the Blackfoot people in Canada carries the same sacred significance as in the American context, but with particular emphasis on the vast prairie landscapes of southern Alberta and Saskatchewan. Among the Blackfoot Confederacy's Canadian members, particularly the Kainai, Siksika, and Piikani nations, the Hawk Spirit is intimately connected to the seasonal rhythms of the northern plains. The spirit is believed to have guided the Blackfoot people across the landscape since time immemorial, showing them where buffalo herds grazed and where water could be found during drought. Its role as protector and guide is especially pronounced in Canadian Blackfoot oral traditions, where stories of the Hawk Spirit's interventions are passed down through generations In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Blackfoot spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous records.

name: Heinzelmännchen
description: The Heinzelmännchen are legendary household spirits from Cologne, Germany, akin to brownies or hobgoblins in other European traditions. These diminutive helpers were said to perform all the household and workshop tasks of Cologne's citizens during the night, allowing the lazy inhabitants of the city to enjoy their days in complete leisure. The legend was first recorded in writing by Cologne teacher Ernst Weyden in 1826 and later popularized by poet August Kopisch in 1836, whose ballad about the Heinzelmännchen became immensely popular and cemented these creatures in German folklore. According to tradition, the Heinzelmännchen worked tirelessly until a tailor's wife, driven by curiosity, scattered peas on the workshop floor to catch them. When they slipped and fell, they fled in anger, never to return
source: German folklore — Heinzelmännchen household spirits documented in German oral tradition.

name: Heksa Barbro
description: Heksa Barbro (Barbro Osmundsdatter) is the legendary witch of Lista in Sørlandet, one of the last people executed for witchcraft in the Lister district. Barbro was burned at Engøy, Farsund, in the 1660s for causing deaths, illness, and cattle bewitching through sorcery. According to local legend, Barbro escaped the execution fire by throwing a thread into the air and flying away on it. Her cave, Poddelopte-hula near Drange, is still a local landmark. A gate in Farsund is named after her — Barbrosporten. The legend says she continues to haunt the Lista area, appearing as an old woman in the heath landscape. She represents the tragic intersection of old Sami-influenced magic traditions and Christian persecution in Sørlandet. The Lista region has an unusually dense concentration of witch trial history, with Barbro as its most famous figure
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Hestenøkken
description: Hestenøkken (the water horse, also known as nøkk-hesten) is the horse-form of the nøkk water spirit in Norwegian folklore, particularly associated with the lakes and fjords of Hardanger and Sogn in Vestlandet. The hestenøkken appears as a beautiful, pure white horse grazing peacefully by the water's edge. When someone approaches to ride it, the horse waits until they are mounted, then gallops straight into the deepest part of the lake or fjord, drowning the rider. The horse is impossible to dismount once ridden — the rider's hands stick to its mane. Unlike the humanoid nøkk who lures with music, the hestenøkken uses the universal appeal of a fine horse to tempt victims. The hestenøkken can also appear as a saddled horse tied to a tree, inviting theft. Legends warn that any strange white horse found near water should be regarded with suspicion
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Hestmannen
description: Hestmannen (the Horseman) is a troll from Nordland folklore, the wild son of Vågakallen of Lofoten. Hestmannen was known for his uncontrollable temper and wild riding. According to legend, he pursued Lekamøya (the Leka Maid) across Vestfjorden on horseback, intending to capture her. As the sun rose, he shot an arrow at her — but Skarsfjellgubben threw his hat in the way, deflecting the arrow. The arrow pierced the hat, creating the famous hole through Torghatten mountain. Hestmannen and his horse were turned to stone by the sunrise at the Arctic Circle. The Hestmannen rock formation is a distinctive landmark on the island of Lurøy/Rødøy in Nordland. The legend is part of the cycle of Seven Sisters stories that explain the geography of the Helgeland coast. Hestmannen represents wild, uncontrolled masculine power in Norwegian folk tradition
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: High John the Conqueror
description: High John the Conqueror is a legendary figure in African American folklore, a trickster hero and spirit of liberation who moved invisibly among the enslaved. According to traditions collected by Zora Neale Hurston, High John was an African prince sold into slavery whose spirit could never be broken. When the whip fell, John would 'take the spirit of his people out of their bodies' so they could not feel the pain. He could be heard laughing in the slave quarters, a sound that reminded the enslaved that freedom was coming. After emancipation, John returned to Africa, but according to Hurston, 'He left his power here' in the root of a certain plant. The dried root of Ipomoea purga, called High John the Conqueror root, is carried in mojo bags for protection, luck, and empowerment in Hoodoo practice
source: Zora Neale Hurston, High John de Conquer (1943)

name: Hiisi
description: Hiisi is a complex figure from Finnish mythology whose meaning evolved dramatically over time. Originally, the term hiisi referred to sacred natural sites: groves, hills, rock formations, and bodies of water where the ancient Finns performed rituals and made offerings. With the Christianization of Finland, these pagan sacred places were demonized, and hiisi transformed from a neutral or positive sacred concept into a malevolent spirit or demon associated with bad luck, illness, and death. In later folklore, hiidet (plural) are depicted as trickster-like entities, often the autochthonous pagan inhabitants of the land, similar to mythological giants. They are associated with salient geographical features and rough terrain, and appear frequently in the Kalevala epic as forces of chaos and mischief that heroes must overcome or outwit
source: Finnish mythology, Kalevala compiled by Elias Lönnrot

name: Hiisi Portti (Hiisi's Gate)
description: Hiisi Portti (Hiisi's Gate) is a phenomenon from Finnish folklore representing a supernatural portal that connects the human world to the realm of Hiisi and other dark spirits. These gates are not architectural structures but rather manifestations that appear at specific times and places, typically in deep forests, at crosswords, or near ancient sacred sites associated with Hiisi. The concept of the Hiisi Gate reflects the Finnish folk belief that the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is permeable at certain liminal moments and locations. Hiisi's Gate is considered extremely dangerous, as those who pass through may find themselves trapped in the spirit realm, unable to return, or may return transformed in body or mind. The gate is both a literal folklore element and a metaphor for the dangers of venturing too far from the safety of human community
source: Finnish mythology, Kalevala compiled by Elias Lönnrot

name: Hinn
description: The Hinn are a class of pre-Adamite supernatural beings from Arabian and Saudi folklore, believed to have inhabited the earth before both humans and jinn. According to Ibn Kathir and other Islamic scholars, the Hinn were among the earliest races created, made from air or subtle fire. They were followed by the Binn (created from water), then the jinn, and finally humans. The Hinn and Binn waged wars and caused corruption on earth, leading the angels to question God's plan to create humanity. Eventually, the jinn were given power over the Hinn and destroyed them. In Bedouin tradition, the Hinn persist as animal-linked spirits that take the form of foxes, wolves, sand cats, and birds of prey — guardians and tricksters that live at the edge of human habitation. They are associated with liminal spaces: the scrub between salt flats, ridges where ibex sleep, and reed fringes. The Hinn represent a covenant between humans and the wild, teaching stewardship of nature
source: Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wal-Nihaya; Ibn Ashur, al-Tahrir wal-Tanwir; FabulaHub; Bedouin oral traditions

name: Hinnøygubben
description: Hinnøygubben (the Old Man of Hinnøya) is a troll from the folklore of the Lofoten/Vesterålen region. According to legend, Hinnøygubben fought with Vågakallen, the troll king of Lofoten, over grazing rights for their reindeer on the border between their territories. During the battle, Hinnøygubben lost his balance and struck his massive axe into the mountain, carving out the Trollfjorden (Trollfjord) — one of the most dramatic and narrow fjords in Norway. Both he and Vågakallen were turned to stone at sunrise, frozen in their battle poses. The Trollfjorden is a real fjord on the border of Lofoten and Vesterålen, famous for its narrow, steep-sided entrance. The battle between the two troll kings explains the dramatic geography of the region. Hinnøygubben represents the wild territoriality of the trolls who shaped the Norwegian landscape
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Hitra-Kjempen
description: Hitra-Kjempen (the Hitra Giant) is a legendary giant said to have lived on the island of Hitra, the largest island in Trøndelag (568 square kilometers). According to local tradition, the Hitra-Kjempen was a solitary giant who was so large that he used entire skerries as stepping stones when walking to the mainland. The giant was known for his enormous appetite — he could eat an entire herd of cattle in one meal — and for throwing boulders at ships he disliked. Various geological features on Hitra are explained through the giant's actions: deep valleys are where he dragged his club, large boulders are stones he threw, and the many small islands around Hitra are crumbs that fell from his catch. The Hitra-Kjempen was eventually tricked by a clever farmer who challenged him to a contest of strength and then used wit to defeat him, a common motif in Norwegian giant legends. The giant's burial mound is said to be located somewhere in the interior of Hitra
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Hmong Creation Spirits (Nkauj Ntsuab & Sis Nab)
description: The Hmong Creation Spirits are the primordial beings from the Hmong creation myth who repopulated the earth after a great flood destroyed humanity. According to the legend, a great argument between the Sky Father (Saub) and the Earth led to a devastating flood. Only two siblings — a brother and sister — survived by taking refuge inside a hollow gourd or a wooden funeral drum that floated on the waters. After the flood receded, they found themselves alone on a mountain peak. The brother proposed marriage to continue the race, but the sister refused. After consulting the spirit world, they were told to roll two millstones down opposite sides of the mountain; if the stones met at the bottom, they were meant to marry. The stones rolled and met at the valley floor, and the siblings married. The sister gave birth to a strange gourd-like mass, which they cut open, releasing all the different peoples of the earth — including the Hmong, Chinese, and Lao. This legend is the Hmong explanation for the diversity of humanity and their own ethnic identity
source: Hmong oral tradition, Hmong shamanic texts

name: Hoggar Mountain Spirits (Kel Ahaggar)
description: The Hoggar Mountain spirits are supernatural beings from the beliefs of the Kel Ahaggar (Tuareg) people of the Hoggar Mountains in southern Algeria. These high peaks, including Mount Tahat (the highest in Algeria), are considered inhabited by powerful spirits that control the weather, protect grazing grounds, and guard hidden treasures. The Hoggar is considered a sacred landscape. Each mountain, pass, and spring has its own spirit. The most powerful is the spirit of Mount Tahat, who controls the rain. The spirits are masters of illusion, leading travelers astray with mirages. They are neither good nor evil but demand respect and are easily offended by littering, shouting, or polluting water sources. They appear as majestic rams with crystal horns, columns of mist, or tall veiled figures on the peaks
source: Tuareg oral tradition, Kel Ahaggar beliefs

name: Horagállis
description: Horagállis (also Dearpmis, Bajanolmmái) is the Sami thunder god, considered one of the most powerful beings in Sami cosmology. Horagállis controls thunder, lightning, rain, and hail — and through these, life and death on the tundra. He is a parallel figure to the Norse Thor but distinctively Sami in character. Horagállis is both creator and destroyer: his lightning brings life-giving rain but also kills those who disrespect him. Noaidi (Sami shamans) would invoke Horagállis for protection during storms and for victory in conflict. Sacred sites dedicated to Horagállis are marked by unusually shaped stones struck by lightning. Offerings of reindeer antlers and silver were left at these sites. Horagállis was particularly feared and respected in the thunder-prone mountain regions of Troms and Finnmark. The name combines elements meaning thunder and old man
source: Sami mythology; Horagállis is the thunder god and one of the most powerful spirits in Sami belief.

name: Horagalles
description: Horagalles is the thunder god in Sami shamanism, one of the most powerful deities in the Sami pantheon. His name likely means 'Thor-man' (from Norse Thor and Sami galles 'old man'), showing Norse influence, though he has deep indigenous roots called Tiermes or Dierpmis among eastern and northern Sami. He rules over thunder and lightning, the rainbow (his bow), weather, oceans, lakes, and human life, health, and well-being. He is depicted on shaman drums with a hammer or two crossed hammers — with one hammer he makes thunder and lightning, with the other he withdraws them to prevent harm. Idols of Horagalles were made of wood with a nail or spike in the head and a piece of flint, holding a hammer called Wetschera. He punishes evil spirits (trolls) who haunt rocks and mountains, destroying them with lightning or dashing their brains out with his hammer. In eastern Sami eschatology, he is a heavenly hunter who pursues a celestial elk/reindeer across the sky — when he shoots it with a fiery arrow, the world will collapse in flames, the stars will fall, and the sun and moon will go out
source: Wikipedia (Horagalles); SNL.no; ancientpages.com; samimuseum.fi

name: Hrosshvalur
description: Hrosshvalur (Horse-Whale) is among the most dreaded of the illhveli (evil whales) in Icelandic folklore. It has a horse-like head with a flowing red mane, a horse's tail, and huge eyes — so large it was sometimes called Monoculus (one-eyed). Hrosshvalur is 15-40 meters long and delights in sinking ships by leaping onto them or whipping up waves with its tail. Eating its flesh is forbidden — it boils away in the pot and cannot be cooked. The Grágás law code banned the eating of hrosshvalur meat. In Kormáks saga, the witch Dorveig transforms into a hrosshvalur to attack a ship. The hrosshvalur neighs like a horse, giving away its presence before it attacks. It represents the uniquely Icelandic classification of whales into edible (nauðvalir) and inedible evil whales (illhveli), a taxonomy found nowhere else
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Hughaman
description: Hughaman (also Hughamar) is a wraith-like doppelganger spirit from the folklore of Setesdal in Sørlandet. The name comes from hug (mind/soul) and ham (shape/form) — the spirit is the soul-form of a person seen before or after death. Seeing one's own hughaman foretells imminent death. Seeing another person's hughaman means that person will soon die or is in mortal danger. The hughaman appears as an exact copy of the person — same clothes, same mannerisms — but is always silent and casts no shadow. Unlike the Norwegian fylgje (a guardian animal spirit), the hughaman is specifically a human doppelganger and is always an omen of death. The hughaman was particularly feared in Setesdal's isolated farm communities. Multiple entries in Johannes Skar's Gamalt or Setesdal catalog the hughaman as one of the most common supernatural experiences in the valley
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Huldufólk
description: Huldufólk (the Hidden People) are the most pervasive supernatural beings in Faroese folklore — a parallel race living just beyond human sight. Unlike Icelandic hidden folk (often beautiful and slender), the Faroese version is consistently described as unusually large in build, with black hair and somber grey clothing. Their dwellings are in ancient burial mounds (álvheyggjur), the most famous being the elf-mound in Norðstreymoy south of Haldórsvík. The huldufólk keep livestock that graze invisibly among human flocks, and fishermen have reported seeing their boats at sea before they vanish. They hate electricity, church bells, and crosses. Anyone who throws stones at a mound risks their wrath — illness, bad luck, or having their children swapped for a changeling. Road construction in the Faroe Islands has been rerouted around known huldufólk dwellings as recently as the 20th century In Faroe Islands folklore, this figure is known among the Faroe Islands people.
source: Faroese folk belief and ethnographic records of island traditions.

Anyone who throws stones at a mound risks their wrath — illness, bad luck, or having their children swapped for a changeling. Road construction in the Faroe Islands has been rerouted around known huldufólk dwellings as recently as the 20th century
source: Jón Árnason, "Íslenzkar Þjóðsögur og Æfintýri" (1862); Icelandic folklore archives

name: Hundred-Egg Children (Bách Việt)
description: The Hundred-Egg Children (Bách Việt) are the mythical founding ancestors of the Vietnamese people, born from an egg sac laid by the mountain fairy Âu Cơ after her marriage to the dragon lord Lạc Long Quân. According to the creation myth, Âu Cơ gave birth to a sac containing one hundred eggs, which hatched into one hundred sons — the progenitors of all Vietnamese people. Due to the elemental incompatibility between the dragon father (water and sea) and the fairy mother (mountains and sky), the couple separated. Fifty sons followed their father to the coast where they learned fishing, sailing, and tattooing; fifty followed their mother to the highlands where they learned farming, animal husbandry, and forest craft. The eldest son became the first Hùng King, founding the Hồng Bàng dynasty that tradition says ruled for 18 generations. The hundred children became the ancestors of the Bách Việt (Hundred Yue) tribes, explaining both the unity and diversity of the Vietnamese people
source: Vietnamese myth, Lĩnh Nam chích quái (14th century)

name: Ifriqiya (Tunisian Serpent of Wisdom)
description: Ifriqiya is a legendary serpent or dragon of Tunisian folklore, named after the ancient Roman province of Africa Proconsularis (which covered modern Tunisia). In Tunisian folk tales, Ifriqiya is said to be the guardian of the land of Tunisia, a wise and ancient serpent that has lived since before the Arab conquest. It is sometimes conflated with the Roman era legend that a giant serpent guarded the granaries of Carthage. Unlike European dragons, Ifriqiya is not necessarily malevolent; snip it is a creature of wisdom and ancient knowledge. It sleeps beneath the earth and its movements cause earthquakes. Some legends say the city of Tunis was built over its head, and if the serpent ever awakens fully, the city will be destroyed. The story shares themes with the Phoenician (Canaanite) serpent Lotan and the Greek Python
source: Tunisian oral tradition, Maghrebi folklore, Roman-era North African legends

name: Ifrit (Powerful Fire Jinn)
description: The Ifrit (plural: Afarit) is a powerful class of jinn in Algerian Islamic folklore, considered among the most dangerous and formidable of supernatural beings. Created from smokeless fire like all jinn, ifrits are distinguished by their immense strength, speed, and malevolent nature. In Algerian tradition, ifrits inhabit desolate places such as ruins, desert wastes, and cemeteries. They are particularly associated with the vast Sahara regions of southern Algeria. Unlike ordinary jinn who may be either good or evil, ifrits are almost always depicted as malevolent, rebellious spirits who actively work against humans. They are known for their incredible speed, ability to lift enormous weights, and their capacity to cause possession, madness, and death. In Islamic scripture, an ifrit is mentioned in the Quran as offering to carry the throne of the Queen of Sheba to King Solomon. In Algerian folk belief, ifrits are especially active at night and are blamed for sudden illnesses, accidents, and unexplained phenomena. Traditional protection involves reciting specific Quranic verses, wearing amulets, and avoiding certain locations at certain times
source: Wikipedia; Quranic references; Algerian oral traditions

name: Imehornets underjordiske
description: Imehornets underjordiske is a supernatural being from the Ime area near Mandal in Sørlandet, famous for offering the legendary Imehornet drinking horn. According to the classic horn legend (ML 6045), two riders passed the Ime farm and were offered a drink by an underground being who emerged from a burial mound. The being offered a magnificent drinking horn. One rider threw the drink over his shoulder — it burned the hide off his horse where it fell. The riders escaped with the horn. The Imehornet is a real artifact now held at the Cultural History Museum in Oslo. The horn likely dates from the 1500s. There are 21 documented Sørlandet variants of this legend, all following the same pattern: a burial mound opens, a being emerges offering a drink, the drink is rejected, and the horn is stolen. The Imehornet variant is the most famous and represents the Sørlandet tradition of mound-dwelling beings
source: Scandinavian folklore; the Underjordiske (hidden people) are nature spirits living in a parallel world.

name: Irrbloss
description: Irrbloss, meaning "wandering blaze" in Swedish, are ghostly flickering lights seen at night in marshes, bogs, and ancient roads. In Swedish folklore they are most commonly believed to be the restless souls of the dead who were neither good enough for heaven nor evil enough for hell, condemned to wander the earth with only a faint light to guide them. Also called Lyktgubbe (lantern man), they are often described as a small man carrying a lantern who leads travelers astray. The Irrbloss can be either malevolent or helpful depending on how they are treated: offering a coin may earn safe passage home, while following them without permission leads to being hopelessly lost in swamps and marshes. Some traditions hold that they guard hidden treasure, and a clever person can trick them with iron to claim the hoard. In southern Sweden they were said to be the souls of wrongdoers such as farmers who harvested crops on stolen land
source: Swedish folklore

name: Bo Usu
description: Bo Usu are powerful forest spirits in Baoulé mythology of Ivory Coast that inhabit the 'bo' — the forest corridors lining streams and rivers, as distinct from the open savannah. These supernatural beings, described as genies, pixies, and entities with magical powers, are specifically invoked by hunters to ensure successful hunts. Hunters commission specialized wooden statuettes called Bo Usu figures, which are intentionally carved with a coarse, rugged aesthetic featuring prominent human sexual anatomy and anthropomorphic features. These figures are treated with sacrificial bird blood, eggshell pieces, and kaolin dust to activate their spiritual power. After a successful hunt, hunters offer animal entrails to the Bo Usu spirits as thanks. The Bo Usu represent the Baoulé belief that the forest is inhabited by powerful non-human intelligences that must be respected and propitiated for humans to safely exploit its resources. These figures are placed at multiple locations outside the hunter's home to attract prey
source: Baoulé oral tradition

name: Gbekre
description: Gbekre is a powerful spirit-deity of the Baoulé people of Ivory Coast, often depicted as a baboon-like figure serving as a judge of souls and protector against evil forces. Unlike the refined, polished ancestor statues typical of Baoulé art, Gbekre figures are intentionally rough-hewn and coarse, combining human and animal features in a deliberately unsettling manner. This crudeness is symbolic of Gbekre's role as a 'humbler' deity who judges the dead and protects the living against sorcerers and malevolent spirits. Gbekre figures, also known as bowl-bearing monkey figures, are used in various cult practices including trance divination, the Mbra society rituals, and as protective talismans against witchcraft. The name 'gbekre' actually means 'mouse' in the Baoulé language, though early French ethnographers mistakenly identified these figures as 'baboon gods.' Despite this etymological confusion, Gbekre remains an important spirit in Baoulé cosmology, associated with judgment, protection, and the enforcement of moral order
source: Baoulé oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Zankallala
description: Zankallala is a remarkable trickster figure from Hausa folklore, found across the Sahel region including northern Ivory Coast. Despite being only the size of two clenched fists, Zankallala is one of the most powerful beings in Hausa mythology, carrying a snake as a walking stick, wearing a pair of scorpions as spurs, and a swarm of bees as a hat. He rides a jerboa into battle and wherever he goes, he is followed by birds that sing his praises and attack his enemies. The most famous story of Zankallala involves his confrontation with the Dodo, the terrifying Swallower-of-Men. After a boy fleeing from a Dodo encounters Zankallala, the tiny hero allows himself to be swallowed three times, each time emerging unscathed from the monster's body until he kills it from within. This story exemplifies the Hausa tradition of the small and clever triumphing over the large and powerful through wit and courage
source: Hausa oral tradition

name: Jólakötturinn
description: Jólakötturinn (the Yule Cat) is a gigantic black cat from Icelandic Christmas folklore, the pet of Grýla and the Yule Lads. The Yule Cat roams the Icelandic countryside on Christmas Eve, eating anyone who has not received new clothes before Christmas. The tradition is tied to the Icelandic wool industry — farmers would give new clothes to workers who finished processing the autumn wool before Christmas. Lazy workers received nothing and thus risked being eaten by the Yule Cat. The cat is described as enormous — the size of a house — with glowing yellow eyes. Its first definitive mention appears in Jón Árnason's 1862 folklore collection, and it was popularized by Jóhannes úr Kötlum's 1932 poem Jólakötturinn. The Yule Cat is now one of Iceland's most internationally recognized folklore figures, alongside Grýla and the Yule Lads
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Jøtul
description: Jøtul (also spelled jotne, jotun; plural: jøtuler) is the Norwegian folk term for the giants of Norse mythology and later Norwegian folklore. In Old Norse, the jötnar (singular: jötunn) were the primordial giants, enemies of the gods, living in Jotunheim. In later Norwegian folklore, the jøtul evolved into a mountain-dwelling giant more like a large troll. Jøtuler are enormous - as tall as mountains - and possess immense strength. They throw boulders at each other across valleys (creating scree fields) and turn to stone if caught by sunlight. Many Norwegian landscape features are explained as jøtul activities - boulders they dropped, mountains they shaped, fjords they carved. The Jotunheimen mountain range is named after them. In folk tradition, jøtuler are more primitive and less magical than trolls, but also more ancient and powerful
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Jab Jab
description: Jab Jab (meaning Double Devil in French Creole, from 'Diable Diable') is a central figure in Grenada's Carnival and folklore traditions. Unlike most Caribbean spirits that are purely mythological, Jab Jab is a costumed Carnival character representing the devil — but in a uniquely Grenadian context. Performers cover themselves in grease or paint, wear chains, and carry whips, embodying the spirit of rebellion and freedom. The Jab Jab tradition has roots in the post-emancipation period when formerly enslaved people used Carnival to satirize and invert the power structures of colonial society. The character is both a fearsome mythological figure — a devil spirit that roams during Carnival — and a powerful symbol of Grenadian resistance and cultural identity. The chains represent slavery, and the whipping movements symbolize breaking free from oppression
source: Grenadian oral and Carnival tradition; snip Island Learning Grenada; snip TravelTips.org

name: Jábmiidáhkká
description: Jábmiidáhkká (Jabme-akka) is the female ruler of Jábmiidaibmu, the Sami underworld of the dead. She is the major chthonic deity in Sami religion, governing the realm where the dead reside. Jábmiidaibmu was not a place of punishment but resembled the world of the living — the dead continued their lives much as before. However, the dead missed their living relatives, and Jábmiidáhkká sometimes allowed them to cause diseases among the living. If a dead soul managed to catch a living person's soul and drag it to the underworld, that person would fall into a coma or fatal illness. Jábmiidáhkká could permit the soul to return if sufficient offerings were made. Black animals — especially cats and roosters — were sacrificed to her by being buried alive under piles of stones. She was ambivalent rather than evil, a necessary figure governing the cycle of life and death. Christian influence later equated her realm with purgatory and associated her with the Virgin Mary. Finnish scholar Kaarle Krohn compared her to Hel from Norse mythology and Louhi from Finnish mythology
source: Wikipedia (Jábmiidáhkká); saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; worldmythos.com

name: Jambavan (King of the Bears)
description: Jambavan is the king of the bears (rikshas) in Hindu texts, a chiranjivi (immortal being) who has lived through multiple cosmic ages. He emerged from the mouth of Brahma when the creator deity yawned, making him one of the first created beings. He was present at the churning of the ocean (Samudra Manthana) and circled the dwarf avatar Vamana 21 times in a single leap when Vishnu measured the three worlds. In the Ramayana, he was a key advisor to Sugriva and played a crucial role in Hanuman's awakening — it was Jambavan who reminded Hanuman of his dormant divine powers and encouraged him to leap across the ocean to Lanka. He also fought in the war against Ravana, serving as a strategist and healer. In the Mahabharata and Bhagavata Purana, Jambavan fought Krishna for 27/28 days over the Syamantaka jewel before recognizing Krishna's divinity, surrendering the gem, and offering his daughter Jambavati in marriage to Krishna
source: Valmiki Ramayana, Mahabharata, Bhagavata Purana, Hindu mythology
